messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Jeweler
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Maladaptive Strategies: Downward Comparison: I remind myself it could have been worse, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David sits with his back pressed so firmly into the corner of the chair that the wooden frame digs into his spine. It is a necessary discomfort. From here, he can see the entire therapy room, the door, the window, the single exit. Six months have passed since his return from a humanitarian posting, but for David, the sense of imminent threat has only intensified. The quiet, meticulous world of a jeweler, which he had longed for during his entire deployment, now feels like a cage lined with invisible tripwires. The trauma had occurred on a brutally hot afternoon at a food distribution point. An explosion in the nearby market had sent a surge of panicked civilians toward their compound. David remembers the dust, the screaming, and the suffocating press of bodies. He was trying to help a small girl who had been separated from her parents when a secondary blast, closer this time, threw him to the ground. The memory is not a coherent narrative but a series of sensory fragments that feel more real than his present reality. He recalls the deafening sound, the sudden, violent shove of a terrified man trying to flee—an unexpected touch that felt like an attack—and the high-pitched, desperate wail of the child he had just been holding. Most of all, he remembers the wild, percussive hammering of his own heart, a frantic rhythm he was certain meant he was about to die.

Back home in his workshop, these fragments ambush him without warning. The sound of children playing in the park across the street can instantly flood him with a paralyzing dread, forcing him to slam the window shut. It’s not a memory of the child’s cry; it is the cry itself, echoing in the small, silent room. At other times, the feeling comes without an image. He will be setting a stone, his focus absolute, and suddenly be engulfed by that same wave of raw terror from the compound, his palms sweating and his stomach clenching for a reason his conscious mind cannot grasp. His own body has become the most unpredictable source of these intrusions. If he takes the stairs too quickly or drinks a strong coffee, the resulting acceleration of his heartbeat is no longer just a physiological response; it is the immediate prelude to catastrophe, the somatic echo of the blast. He has come to believe his own body is a traitor, ready to betray him into panic at any moment.

To cope, David has developed a rigid set of rules. He scans every room he enters, his eyes instinctively cataloging potential weapons—a heavy glass vase on a reception desk, a letter opener, the thick leg of a chair. He tells himself it could have been worse, that he was lucky to get out with only scratches. He forces himself to think of the beautiful, intricate rings he has designed, trying to overlay the positive thoughts on the churning anxiety, but it feels like placing a fine silk cloth over a landmine. His world has shrunk. A friendly pat on the back from an old acquaintance sent him stumbling away with a choked cry, an overreaction that shattered the conversation and left him deeply ashamed. He no longer meets friends for drinks, unable to bear the casual jostling of a crowd or the impossibility of finding a seat where he can watch every entrance. His work, once a source of pride and calm, is now a source of constant tension. His hands, which need to be rock-steady for fine engraving, often tremble. He ruined a custom engagement ring last month when a car backfired on the street, causing him to flinch and gouge the setting. That was when he knew he couldn't manage this on his own. He is here now because he is terrified of losing the one thing he thought would be his refuge. He wants to feel safe in his own workshop, to trust the reassurances of others, and more than anything, to experience his own heartbeat as a simple sign of life, not an alarm signaling his imminent death.
